newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Kissinger sees no Chinese expansionism.
newsitem.headline: Kissinger sees no Chinese expansionism.

text.p: Former U.S. Secretary of State Henry Kissinger said on Tuesday that China's preoccupation with domestic issues would deter its military from engaging in expansionist moves.
Kissinger, on a four-day visit to the Philippines, said economic globalisation made it possible for nations to raise living standards by developing their own societies without resorting to conquests.

"I don't know what China will do in 10 to 15 years...but I also believe that there is so much to be done inside China that military conquest is a less likely, the least likely, consequence of Chinese growth," he said in a speech.
Kissinger, who helped establish U.S. ties with China in the 1970s, spoke at the state-run University of the Philippines during a ceremony in which he was awarded an honorary doctor of laws degree.
He said Americans were involved in a debate to define the U.S. role in the world and that whenever he travelled to Asia he was asked what the United States' plan was for the region.
"There is a certain missionary spirit in America and we have a tendency to mix excessively in domestic affairs," he said.

"You have to remember that we are a young nation only 200 years old and that when we deal with countries like China or India we tend to forget that they managed to get along for 5,000 years without advice from the United States."
He said this inclination was linked to the United States being the only major power with a population almost entirely composed of immigrants.

"Because so many Americans came as immigrants -- as a matter of fact, I did -- and because they turned their backs on the countries from which they came, Americans have a tendency to believe that our domestic organisation could be exported to every other part of the world," Kissinger said.
In the Philippines, a U.S. colony for nearly 50 years until 1946, American-style democracy took strong roots, he said.
"But in many other countries of Asia one came up against long traditions of different ideas of domestic organisation," he added.
